final_answer:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL - ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
MEMORANDUM - Breach Notification Obligations, EvergreenConnect Incident (EHS-IR-2025-002)
To: David Yoon (GC); Dr. Maren Haskell (CPO). Cc: R. Calloway. As of May 19, 2025. Statutory text to be cite-checked before filing; HHS constructive-discovery risk before May 2 (patch 27 days overdue) is noted.

1. BOTTOM LINE
(a) Treat May 2, 2025 as the discovery date for every purpose. (b) Notices are already late or imminent: BAA 5-business-day incident report (May 9), Oregon and Florida vendor-to-client notices (10 days, May 12), and 30-day state clocks (CO, FL, WA, NY) expiring about June 1 (a Sunday, so work to Friday May 30). (c) The "Evergreen is a Covered Entity for 9,400 telehealth patients" premise is weak on our own documents; plan for Evergreen as Business Associate (BA) for all 83,400 while preparing a protective direct-notice option. (d) The state chart in the May 19 spreadsheet contains material errors (Section 5). (e) Do not use a single letter. (f) Notification cost is roughly double the policy limit and needs insurer consent before commitment.

2. DISCOVERY DATE AND CLOCKS
HIPAA: a breach is "discovered" on the first day it is known, or by reasonable diligence would have been known, to the entity or any workforce member or agent (45 CFR 164.404(a)(2) for covered entities; 164.410(a)(2) for BAs). The SOC alert at 2:17 AM on May 2, escalated to the CISO by 2:23 AM, satisfies this. Policy HIPAA-BN-2025-004 Sec. 2 and 4.3 define discovery as the Privacy Officer's determination; that definition conflicts with the regulation, cannot bind HHS, and should be amended (and the Appendix A form revised). The BAA does not help us either: BAA 1.2(b) adopts the regulatory knowledge standard, and Policy Sec. 1 says the more restrictive obligation controls.
Key deadlines from May 2: BAA 4.1 successful-incident report, 5 business days = May 9 (missed unless the May 3 contact Lakeshore references qualifies; see 4); OR and FL vendor notice 10 days = May 12; BAA 4.3 CE notice June 1; CO, FL, WA, NY 30 days = June 1; OH, OR, WI 45 days = June 16; HIPAA, CT, LA outer limit 60 days = July 1 (HIPAA standard is "without unreasonable delay"; 60 days is a ceiling, not a safe harbor). Texas runs from determination (June 15 if May 16; use May 30 to be safe; AG within 30 days).
Agency risk: if a CE client treats Evergreen as its agent, Evergreen's May 2 knowledge is imputed to the CE and its own 60-day clock started May 2 regardless of when we notify it (HHS 2013 Omnibus Rule preamble, 78 Fed. Reg. 5566, 5656). Evergreen's delay therefore consumes client time and feeds the indemnity claim.

3. EVERGREEN'S HIPAA STATUS: TWO TRACKS, BUT THE CE PREMISE IS WEAK
BA track (312 BAA clients, about 74,000 individuals): Evergreen must notify each CE without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days (164.410), here contractually 30 days (BAA 4.3), with identities of affected individuals and the 164.404(c) content. The CE then owes individual, HHS (164.408) and media (164.406) notice. Spreadsheet and policy transpose the sections: media notice is 164.406; HHS notice is 164.408. BAA 4.5 bars Evergreen from contacting HHS or regulators about a client's PHI without that client's consent.
Telehealth track (about 9,400 individuals): the SaaS agreement makes the client "solely responsible for the patient-provider relationship" (Sec. 2.3), treats patient data as "Client Data" owned by the client (6.2), and sets Authorized Users as client staff. That describes Evergreen as a service provider to the provider, i.e., a BA without a BAA, not a health care provider. Being a "covered entity" requires being a provider that itself conducts standard transactions electronically (160.103); hosting a portal does not do that. Likely result: the telehealth clients are the CEs and Evergreen is a BA in violation of 164.502(e)/164.504(e) (no BAA) and 164.308(b); a BA's duties apply by operation of law (164.410 applies regardless of contract). Note the inconsistent counts: the timeline says 7 affected telehealth clients; the forensic report says 9,400 patients across 35 clients. Verify before sending. Recommendation: (i) notify all telehealth clients now under SaaS 8.2 and 164.410 as BA; (ii) offer to send notices on their behalf by written delegation; (iii) if any client refuses or confirms Evergreen delivered care directly, Evergreen notifies directly as CE. Also fix the known no-BAA gap (risk item #9, flagged November 2024, target Q2 2025): continued inaction after documented knowledge is willful-neglect exposure.

4. WHAT MUST HAPPEN NOW
- Written BA notice to all 312 BAA clients plus telehealth clients, with the 164.404(c) elements, client-level patient lists and data elements. Reconcile Lakeshore's statement that it received "initial incident notification on May 3"; the log shows only a generic May 2 status message and Calloway advising a hold on May 3. If a May 3 notice was given, it starts the CE clock for Lakeshore and may establish compliance with BAA 4.1; if none, Evergreen was in breach on May 9.
- HIPAA allows only law-enforcement delay (164.412); none is documented. Waiting for the May 23 final report is not a basis for delay.
- Offer centralized notification; execute written delegations. A CE remains legally responsible for its own notice (and its state filings). Obtain Northbridge's prior written consent before committing (policy 5.2 bars assumed obligations).
- Individual notice: first-class mail; substitute notice if 10 or more bad addresses (90-day website posting or major media plus toll-free number); content under 164.404(c). Media notice: all 14 states exceed 500 residents (Montana is smallest at 1,500), so prominent outlets in each state; simultaneous release. HHS portal filing contemporaneous with individual notice for each CE (or by Evergreen as delegate).
- Illinois: Lakeshore asks whether Evergreen filed with the Illinois AG; answer in writing that Lakeshore, as the owner of the data, files unless it delegates.

5. STATE MATRIX (corrections to the May 19 spreadsheet marked CORRECTION)
Common rules: where state law applies to a BA, it must notify the data owner (the CE) promptly; many states deem HIPAA-compliant entities compliant for individual notice but still require regulator filings. Each state counts residents with state-defined personal information; SSN-only definitions (WI, OH, LA, MA) cover about 2,800, 2,700, 3,150 and 1,400 SSN-holders respectively, not full counts, but HIPAA covers everyone. The spreadsheet's state SSN column sums to 61,100 and its non-SSN column to 22,300, versus 61,200 and 22,200 elsewhere; reconcile.
- TX (18,200): individuals within 60 days of determination; AG within 30 days if 250+ (Tex. Bus. & Com. Code 521.053, as amended by SB 768). CORRECTION: AG is 30 days, not 60. No "TX HHS" breach filing exists under 521.053.
- CA (12,600): most expedient time, without unreasonable delay (Civ. Code 1798.82); AG sample copy if 500+; HIPAA-compliant notice deemed to satisfy content. CORRECTION: CMIA 56.06 contains no breach-notice duty; the provider-notice duty (Health & Safety Code 1280.15, 15 business days) applies to licensed clinics and facilities; confirm no client is one. CMIA statutory damages (56.36) are a litigation exposure for any client.
- IL (11,200): without unreasonable delay; AG required only if more than 500 residents (815 ILCS 530/10); HIPAA entities must notify AG within 5 business days after notifying HHS (530/50). CORRECTION: not "any number."
- NY (6,100): CORRECTION: as amended December 2024, notice within 30 days of discovery (no tolling for scoping) and notice to AG, Department of State, State Police, and DFS (DFS only if a DFS-covered entity per chapter amendment); medical and health insurance data were added to "private information" in 2025. HIPAA entities notify AG within 5 business days of HHS notice. The spreadsheet omits the 30-day rule and Department of State. Treat as a June 1 deadline.
- FL (5,900): 30 days from determination or reason to believe (extendable 15 days for good cause); Department of Legal Affairs if 500+ within 30 days; third-party agents must notify the covered entity within 10 days (501.171(6)). Evergreen is a third-party agent: the 10 days has run. Deemed-compliant HIPAA notice still requires a copy to the Department.
- OR (4,800): 45 days; AG if more than 250; CORRECTION: a vendor must notify the covered entity within 10 days and itself notify the AG if more than 250 consumers (ORS 646A.604). Evergreen should file as vendor.
- LA (4,300): 60 days; CORRECTION: AG Consumer Protection Section written notice within 10 days of notifying residents, listing affected residents (LAC 16:III.701); the spreadsheet says none.
- WI (3,800): reasonable time, within 45 days (Wis. Stat. 134.98); no AG filing; CRAs if over 1,000. Statute has no express minor or parent provision; Calloway's contrary statement should be verified.
- OH (3,700): 45 days (R.C. 1349.19); no AG filing; CRAs if over 1,000.
- CO (3,400): 30 days from determination; AG if 500+ (C.R.S. 6-1-716).
- CT (3,200): 60 days; AG not later than notice to residents; 24 months identity theft prevention services if SSN involved (36a-701b).
- WA (2,800): 30 days from discovery; AG if more than 500, within 30 days (RCW 19.255.010); BA notifies owner immediately.
- MA (1,900): as soon as practicable; AG and OCABR; CORRECTION to extent needed: resident letters must not describe the nature of the breach or number affected, and must offer at least 18 months credit monitoring if SSN is involved (c. 93H, 3, 3A).
- MT (1,500): without unreasonable delay; CORRECTION: AG Consumer Protection Office must receive a copy simultaneously with resident notice in every case, not only on substitute notice (30-14-1704).
Encryption safe harbor: unavailable. HHS guidance (74 Fed. Reg. 19006) protects only data actually rendered unreadable; the API returned plaintext. The citations "164.402(2)(iv)" in the timeline and policy are wrong; the safe harbor sits in the "unsecured PHI" definition, and (2)(iv) is the fourth risk factor. The same result holds under state statutes.

6. SPECIAL POPULATIONS
Minors (Pine Ridge, 3,800): HIPAA notice goes to the personal representative (164.502(g)); parents or guardians typically. Pine Ridge, as CE, supplies and verifies addresses; Evergreen's "responsible party" field may be stale. Use a parent-directed letter, minor-specific monitoring, and a dedicated call script.
Clearwater (6,100, 42 CFR Part 2): Part 2 applies to the Part 2 program (Clearwater); Evergreen is a qualified service organization/BA. The 2024 final rule (published February 16, 2024; effective April 16, 2024; compliance date February 16, 2026, not February 2024 as the email states) applies the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule to Part 2 records, and no separate SAMHSA filing exists; HHS OCR is the reporting channel. Because the compliance date had not arrived, HIPAA still governs; follow the Part 2 standard anyway. Letters may describe "behavioral health treatment information" without stating SUD, but must still list the data types generally (164.404(c)); NY Mental Hygiene Law and other state confidentiality statutes may add limits; confirm.
Credit monitoring: legally mandated only in CT (24 months) and MA (18 months); BAA 4.4 sets a 12-month floor if requested by the CE. Offering 24 months to all 61,200 is a business decision.

7. COST, INSURANCE, INDEMNITY
Estimated response cost is about $19.0M (credit monitoring alone $17.6M) against a $10M limit and $250K SIR. Policy: claims-made-and-reported, expires June 30, 2025; keep all related claims noticed, seek insurer consent for Apex and Sentinel (non-panel), no admissions. BAA 7.1 indemnity is uncapped and likely uninsured under the contractual-liability exclusion. Calloway's no-concession approach is right; avoid statements about cause in client letters. 

8. ACTION LIST
1. Adopt May 2 as discovery; amend policy. 2. Send BA notices to all clients by May 21-23. 3. Make OR (vendor) and LA, FL, NY, CO, WA, TX filings per schedule above; target mailings and HHS portal by May 30. 4. Resolve BA/CE status of telehealth with written client positions and BAAs. 5. Pine Ridge address verification. 6. Obtain insurer consent. 7. Reconcile counts (SSN, 9,400/35 vs 7 clients). 8. Cite-check statutory text before any filing.
